refsection.title: Description
refsection.para: list-logins is a tool for listing login information, taken from the operating system's terminal logins table (which is maintained by commands such as login-update-utx1, utx1, login-process1, login-envuidgid1, login1, getty1, and others). Its output is machine-parseable, being encoded field by field with vis3. The output is suitable for console-flat-table-viewer1 with 1 header line and --format tabbed, or for awk1 with -F'\t', or for mlr1 with its --inidx option.

refsection.title: Login table fields
refsection.para: The --field command‐line option specifies the list of fields to emit. Each field named name is specified by a separate option. What exactly the fields are varies from operating system to operating system. There is a basic common set: line, user, host, and time. These fields are from utmp5; and apart from host, they have a history that goes back to 7th Edition Unix.
refsection.note: It is not an error for name to name a field that does not exist on the current platform. list-logins will simply emit a column with all blank fields in that case. Field names are case sensitive, and in the current implementation there are no field names with any uppercase letters.
refsection.para: Operating systems that implement utmpx5 often add extensions: pid, session, and address. The platforms that supply an address field always supply it as an IP version 6 address. If IP version 4 was used, they supply the field contents as a mapped IP version 6 address. list-logins uses the platform's library to convert IP version 6 addresses to a (vis3‐encoded) human-readable form, and makes no effort to itself guess when and how to display IP version 4 addresses.
refsection.note: Everyone who provides these extra fields also provides utmpx5, so list-logins does not bother with any extensions to utmp5. utmpx5 is the preferred system and is used exclusively if the platform's library is found to support it.
refsection.para: The --time-format command‐line option specifies an alternative display format to be employed for all time fields, formatstring, in the form employed by the strftime3 library function. The default is ISO 8601 date and time, and numeric timezone offset.

refsection.title: Selecting login table records
refsection.para: The line command‐line arguments are a filter set that is matched against the line names, enabling the selection of individual login records. If there are no line arguments, the entire list is output, unfiltered. It is not an error for a filter item not to match a line.

The --no-init command‐line option has no effect on most BSDs, where the concept is meaningless. On Linux-based operating systems, it excludes INIT_PROCESS and LOGIN_PROCESS records, created by login-process1 and the programs that it is compatible with. With modern systems with modern system managers, this option is either meaningless or moot on Linux-based operating systems also.

refsection.title: Output
refsection.para: The output format is variable-length records terminated by LF containing TAB-separated fields. Fields are output as if passed through the BSD vis3 library function. They are thus unambiguously machine-parseable, because any whitespace in the field itself is encoded by vis3. After separating out an individual field, its contents can (for example) be decoded in shell script using the unvis1 utility (which is supplied by FreeBSD).
The field names are transformed to uppercase for the initial header record.

informalexample.para: This command uses list-logins to produce similar output to who1 with its -H option.

literallayout.userinput: awk '{ if (1 == NR) print; else printf "%s\t%s\t%s\t(%s)\n",$1,$2,$3,$4; }' |

informalexample.para: This command uses list-logins to display a continually updated table similar to who1 with its -H option.

literallayout.userinput: while list-logins --field pid --field name --field line --field time --field host |
awk '{ if ( 2 > NR ) printf "\f%s\n",$0; else printf "%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t(%s)\n",$1,$2,$3,$4,$5,$6; }'
